questions.question: What does a base language model learn during autoregressive pretraining?
options: A database of guaranteed facts
A probability distribution for the next token given preceding tokens
A fixed set of product workflows
A deterministic answer for every prompt
questions.explanation: Autoregressive training predicts the next token from prior tokens. Useful capabilities emerge from that objective, but truth and product policy are not guaranteed.

questions.question: Why should training plans balance model size and token count under a fixed compute budget?
options: Parameters are the only source of model quality.
Training data stops mattering once a model is large.
An oversized model trained on too few useful tokens can be a worse use of the same compute.
Every model should use exactly the same token-to-parameter ratio.
questions.explanation: Scaling-law work shows that parameters, data, and compute are coupled. The exact optimum depends on the training setup, so a fixed universal ratio is not the lesson.

questions.question: A private policy corpus changes hourly and answers must cite current authorized text. Which adaptation is the best starting point?
options: Put the policy facts into a preference-tuned checkpoint.
Use request-time retrieval with source and access controls.
Train a new base model every hour.
Increase sampling temperature.
questions.explanation: Retrieval keeps volatile evidence and permissions outside model weights, enabling independent updates, revocation, and source attribution.

questions.question: When is a supervised adapter most defensible?
options: Whenever a prompt can be made shorter
Before any prompt or retrieval baseline is measured
When a stable behavior remains unmet, representative examples exist, and the adapter can be evaluated and rolled back
When facts change every few minutes
questions.explanation: Learned adaptation adds data, training, compatibility, and release burdens. Use it for stable unmet behavior after lighter mechanisms are evaluated.

questions.question: Which change most directly reduces prefill work for requests that share a long stable prefix?
options: Increase the maximum output length.
Reuse a validated prefix cache entry.
Raise concurrency without a memory check.
Add a larger batch wait to every request.
questions.explanation: A correct prefix-cache hit avoids recomputing reusable prompt tokens. Cache identity must include every input that changes the prefix result.

questions.question: Why can long prompts and high concurrency exhaust an inference worker even when model weights fit?
options: The KV cache grows with active sequence context and consumes additional device memory.
Output tokens are stored permanently in model weights.
Tokenization duplicates the model checkpoint for every request.
Attention removes all per-request state.
questions.explanation: Each active sequence needs attention state. Context length, concurrency, architecture, precision, and cache management determine its memory pressure.

questions.question: What is the strongest model release gate?
options: The candidate wins one public benchmark.
The candidate has more parameters than the current model.
The complete system passes versioned task, safety, latency, cost, and failure-slice thresholds with a rollback path.
The average answer is longer.
questions.explanation: A production model is one part of a system. Release evidence must cover representative quality, risk, operations, and rollback, not one aggregate score.
